sentence: It depends on the antibiotic: the NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with common ones, but firm warnings exist for a few.
note: As body[0] and body[1].

sentence: The NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics, though alcohol may worsen side effects such as nausea or dizziness.
note: As body[0] sentences 1 and 2.

sentence: The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and tinidazole, and NHS 111 Wales names linezolid and doxycycline as interacting with alcohol too.
note: As body[1] sentences 2 and 3.

sentence: The NHS says amoxicillin can be taken with alcohol, and that azithromycin can too unless it causes dizziness, although some NHS azithromycin pages are more cautious.
note: As body[4].

sentence: UK sources word the advice differently, so the leaflet in the pack and a pharmacist or GP are the places the NHS points to for a specific antibiotic.
note: As body[5].

sentence: For a serious allergic reaction to an antibiotic, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.
note: As body[6].

sentence: The NHS says that drinking alcohol in moderation is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics.
note: NHS antibiotics interactions page (as summarised): moderate drinking unlikely to cause problems with most common antibiotics; NHS 111 Wales says the same.

sentence: It adds that some antibiotics can cause side effects such as feeling sick or dizzy, and alcohol may make these worse.
note: Same pages: some antibiotics cause nausea or dizziness which alcohol can worsen.

sentence: So the answer depends on which antibiotic has been prescribed.
note: Search summaries: NHS guidance depends on which antibiotic is taken; some have specific alcohol warnings.

sentence: Antibiotics are medicines that treat infections caused by bacteria.
note: Plain textbook definition.

sentence: The NHS interactions page also points people with doubts towards a GP or pharmacist.
note: Summary of the page: check with a GP or pharmacist if unsure; NHS 111 Wales says ask a GP or pharmacist if unsure.

sentence: Alcohol is only one of the things that page covers, because it also deals with how antibiotics can change the way other medicines and herbal supplements work.
note: Search summary of the NHS interactions page: covers other medicines and herbal supplements, food, contraceptive pill and alcohol.

sentence: A small number of antibiotics carry a firmer warning about alcohol.
note: NHS 111 Wales lists metronidazole, tinidazole, linezolid and doxycycline as interacting with alcohol.

sentence: The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and with tinidazole.
note: MC page: do not drink alcohol while taking metronidazole; NHS 111 Wales: avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and tinidazole. Tinidazole's own NHS page was not returned, so tinidazole is attributed to NHS 111 Wales only.

sentence: NHS 111 Wales also names linezolid and doxycycline as antibiotics that interact with alcohol.
note: NHS 111 Wales antibiotics page covers linezolid and doxycycline alongside metronidazole and tinidazole.

sentence: For linezolid, it suggests avoiding drinks made by fermenting, such as wine, beer, sherry and lager.
note: NHS 111 Wales: avoid undistilled fermented drinks such as wine, beer, sherry and lager with linezolid.

sentence: For doxycycline, it says alcohol can affect how well the medicine works.
note: NHS 111 Wales: alcohol can affect how the drug works (summary also said less effective in heavy drinkers; not used here).

sentence: The NHS page of common questions about doxycycline is reported to say that it is best not to drink alcohol with this medicine, because alcohol can stop it working properly.
note: Search 1 summary attributed this to the NHS doxycycline page; the excerpt was not returned verbatim, so treat as lower confidence.

sentence: These are the antibiotics named in the NHS pages retrieved for this guide, not a complete list.
note: Meta statement about scope of the pages retrieved; the pages say to check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist or GP.

sentence: The NHS says that mixing alcohol with metronidazole can cause nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, hot flushes and a fast, pounding heartbeat.
note: NHS common questions about metronidazole: mixing with alcohol can cause nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, hot flushes and a fast or pounding heartbeat.

sentence: The NHS says this advice applies to metronidazole tablets, liquid and suppositories, and its guidance for the vaginal gel is similar.
note: Search summary of NHS metronidazole pages: do not drink alcohol while taking tablets, liquid or using suppositories; vaginal gel guidance similar.

sentence: NHS 111 Wales lists similar effects for metronidazole and tinidazole, including headaches, dizziness and drowsiness.
note: NHS 111 Wales: feeling sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, fast or irregular heartbeat, headaches, dizziness and drowsiness.

sentence: The NHS says the advice to avoid alcohol carries on for a while after the last dose, which gives the medicine time to leave the body.
note: NHS metronidazole pages: continue to avoid alcohol for a period after finishing treatment so the medicine can leave the body (number of days deliberately left out).

sentence: NHS 111 Wales gives a longer wait for tinidazole than for metronidazole.
note: NHS 111 Wales: longer period after stopping tinidazole than after metronidazole.

sentence: Other NHS pages give different lengths of time, so the leaflet or the pharmacist can say which applies.
note: Search summaries: the trichomoniasis treatment page and local NHS leaflets give shorter or different periods; advice to check leaflet or pharmacist.

sentence: Apart from alcohol, the NHS says there is no need to avoid other food or drink with metronidazole.
note: Summary of NHS common questions page: apart from alcohol, eat and drink normally.

sentence: Some antibiotics cause nausea or dizziness, and the NHS says alcohol can make these feelings worse.
note: NHS interactions page and NHS 111 Wales: alcohol may worsen nausea or dizziness caused by some antibiotics.

sentence: For azithromycin, the NHS says that if the medicine makes a person dizzy, alcohol will make them feel worse.
note: NHS common questions about azithromycin: can drink alcohol, but not if the medicine makes you dizzy, as alcohol will make you feel worse.

sentence: The NHS interactions page also says that avoiding alcohol while unwell is generally advised.
note: Search summary of the NHS interactions page: avoiding alcohol while unwell is generally advised, though moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems. Wording comes from a summary, not a verbatim excerpt.

sentence: The NHS pages retrieved here focus on side effects and specific interactions rather than on how fast the body recovers.
note: Meta statement about scope: none of the returned NHS excerpts quantify alcohol's effect on recovery; not a medical claim.

sentence: For that reason this guide does not claim that alcohol slows recovery from infection.
note: Meta statement about what the guide leaves out; not a medical claim.

sentence: Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin family of antibiotics, and azithromycin to the macrolide family.
note: Standard drug classification, also stated on the site's own medicine pages.

sentence: The NHS common questions page for amoxicillin says alcohol can be drunk while taking it.
note: NHS common questions about amoxicillin: you can drink alcohol while taking amoxicillin.

sentence: The same page says no food or drink needs to be avoided with amoxicillin.
note: Summary of NHS amoxicillin page: eat and drink normally.

sentence: For azithromycin, the NHS common questions page says alcohol can be drunk, but not if the medicine causes dizziness.
note: NHS common questions about azithromycin: can drink alcohol; if it makes you dizzy, do not, as it will make you feel worse.

sentence: Two other NHS azithromycin pages, About azithromycin and Side effects of azithromycin, word this more cautiously and say alcohol may make a person feel worse.
note: Search summary: About azithromycin says avoid alcohol as it will make you feel worse; side effects page similar. Wording taken from the summary, not a verbatim excerpt.

sentence: The NHS pages for flucloxacillin, another penicillin, and for ciprofloxacin also say alcohol can be drunk, and the clarithromycin page repeats the caution about dizziness.
note: Search 1 summary: flucloxacillin and ciprofloxacin pages say alcohol allowed; clarithromycin page allows it but advises against if it causes dizziness. Wording from the summary.

sentence: The wording therefore differs between pages for the same medicine, and a pharmacist can say how it applies to a particular prescription.
note: Follows from the differing pages; the pharmacist route is from the NHS interactions page.

sentence: They do not always match.
note: Search summaries: NHS England, NHS inform and a hospital trust leaflet word the advice differently.

sentence: NHS inform, the Scottish NHS information service, says alcohol should not be drunk while taking antibiotics, or for a period after finishing them.
note: NHS inform antibiotics page (as summarised): do not drink alcohol while taking antibiotics or for a period after finishing; the number of hours is deliberately left out.

sentence: NHS 111 Wales gives the same message about moderate drinking as the NHS interactions page, then lists the antibiotics with firmer warnings.
note: NHS 111 Wales: moderate drinking unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics; separate sections for metronidazole, tinidazole, linezolid, doxycycline.

sentence: An NHS hospital trust leaflet says there are no known interactions between most antibiotics and alcohol, while naming a few exceptions.
note: Royal United Hospitals Bath leaflet: no known interactions between most antibiotics and alcohol, but avoid with certain others (summary wording).

sentence: This is why the NHS pages keep returning to the leaflet in the pack and to a pharmacist or GP for the antibiotic in question.
note: Summaries: check the leaflet or ask a GP or pharmacist, especially for metronidazole, tinidazole, linezolid or doxycycline.

sentence: For a question about one antibiotic and alcohol, the NHS points to a pharmacist or GP.
note: NHS interactions page and NHS 111 Wales: ask a GP or pharmacist if unsure.

sentence: NHS guidance on antibiotic side effects says most are mild, but serious allergic reactions need an emergency response.
note: Search 8 summary: most side effects mild; serious allergic reactions need emergency response.

sentence: NHS 111 is the route for urgent advice that cannot wait for a pharmacy or GP appointment.
note: Search summary of antibiotic side effects guidance: get advice from a pharmacist, GP or NHS 111 if there is a reaction. The urgency framing comes from the summary; the page text was not returned verbatim.

sentence: In rare cases an antibiotic can cause anaphylaxis, a severe and potentially life-threatening allergic reaction.
note: NHS antibiotic side effects: in rare cases an antibiotic can cause anaphylaxis.

sentence: For milder allergic-type reactions that do not improve, the NHS suggests contacting a GP.
note: Search 8 summary: mild reactions such as hives usually treated with antihistamines; if symptoms do not improve, contact GP.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for signs such as a skin rash, wheezing, tightness in the chest or throat, trouble breathing or talking, or swelling of the mouth, face, lips, tongue or throat.
note: NHS antibiotics side effects page: call 999 or go to A&E for rash, wheezing, tightness in chest or throat, trouble breathing or talking, swelling of mouth, face, lips, tongue or throat.
